# Potato blight and the risk of monoculture (`potato_blight_monoculture_risk`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/agriculture.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Agriculture & food (`agriculture`)
- Deps: needs potato_cultivation; helped by microorganisms, contagion_theory
- Core idea: A whole people living on one crop of one variety can lose everything in one season. Potato blight is caused by a water mould (an oomycete) whose spores blow from plant to plant in cool wet weather; leaves blacken within days and the tubers rot in the ground or in store. In Ireland in 1845–52, where many poor households depended on susceptible potatoes, particularly the Lumper, about a million died and more than a million emigrated. Defences: several crops and several varieties, healthy seed tubers, earthing up, cutting off the tops at the first black spots, and spraying the leaves before infection with Bordeaux mixture (1 kg copper sulphate and 1 kg slaked lime in 100 litres of water).
- Pitfalls:
  - Blaming wet weather, bad air or 'degeneration' of the plant, as most experts did in 1845; the cause is a parasite
  - Spraying after the leaves are black; copper only protects healthy leaves
  - Treating the famine as a purely natural disaster; grain was exported from Ireland throughout and relief policy decided who died
  - Leaving diseased tubers and tops in heaps beside the field
- History: americas: origin in central Mexico or the Andes (disputed); 1843 outbreaks in the eastern United States; europe: 1845 – appears in Belgium in June, Ireland by September; 1846 M. J. Berkeley argues a fungus is the cause; 1861–63 de Bary proves it; 1882–85 Millardet's Bordeaux mixture
- Read:
  - Cormac Ó Gráda, Black '47 and Beyond: The Great Irish Famine in History, Economy, and Memory (1999)
  - E. C. Large, The Advance of the Fungi (1940)
